svg.title: OCR-then-text retrieval compared with visual retrieval over page images
svg.desc: A hand-drawn comparison of two retrieval pipelines over a stack of page images. The first runs the page image through OCR, chunks the extracted text, embeds one vector per chunk, and retrieves; a caption notes what OCR throws away — a chart becomes a caption, a table becomes a mangled run of numbers, a figure becomes nothing — and that a silent OCR error becomes a confidently wrong answer downstream. The second, visual retrieval as in ColPali, splits the page into image patches, keeps one vector per patch, and scores pages by sum-of-max similarity against the query tokens, never running OCR; it can match a question about a bar chart to the page holding the chart. Two panels give the trade: stay with OCR when pages are clean prose and the text layer is reliable, and reach for visual retrieval when the corpus is visually rich. A caption advises routing per page rather than choosing one method for a whole corpus.
svg.text: Two ways to retrieve over a stack of page images
One runs OCR first and inherits every one of its errors. The other never runs OCR at all.
What OCR throws away: a chart becomes a caption, a table becomes a mangled run of numbers, a figure becomes nothing at all.
A silent OCR error on a poor scan, a rotated page, or an unusual font becomes a confidently wrong answer downstream.
It can match a question about a bar chart to the page holding the chart. OCR-then-text never could, because the chart was never text.
The same late-interaction mechanism as ColBERT in Post 17, lifted from text tokens onto image patches (Faysse et al., 2024).
The pages are mostly clean prose and the text layer is reliable.
Cheaper to index, and the extracted text composes with everything
The corpus is visually rich — slides, dashboards, forms,
figure-heavy papers — and OCR loses information you need. One
vector per patch multiplies the index.
The failure mode to avoid is picking one method for the whole corpus. Real document sets are mixed, so route per page.
Send text-heavy pages as extracted text and layout-heavy pages as pixels, and pay the premium only where layout carries meaning.
